title: I Tried Making Viral Animated Videos With AI (No Coding, No Editing)
title_options: How to Make Viral Animated Explainer Videos With AI (Step by Step)
I Made a 9-Minute Animated YouTube Video Without Editing Anything
description: I tried making the animated "What if" style videos that are everywhere on YouTube right now, without coding, editing or animating anything myself. Here is exactly how, step by step, including what took longest and what it can't do yet.
description_credits: Example 1: "What If Your Reaction Time Was 10x Faster?" by Ifverse (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MroF1XmHOZw), shown for commentary. Not mine.
Example 2: "What If Every Step Made You Twice as Big?" by AFTER THE DOOR (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ylnTesFVoOo), shown for commentary. Not mine.

beats.say: I just made a fully animated YouTube video, with a voice, a story and every scene drawn,
and I didn't write code, I didn't edit a single clip, and I can't animate.
When you see it, you'll think it took days of work.
It didn't. Let me show you exactly how I did it.
If you've been on YouTube lately, you've seen these animated "What if" videos.
This one by Ifverse has over four and a half million views.

proof.title: What If Your Reaction Time Was 10x Faster?

beats.say: And this one by After the Door has over two point three million.

proof.title: What If Every Step Made You Twice as Big?

beats.say: Those aren't mine. But they show something important: people watch these all the way through, because each one is a question they actually want answered.
And I know how-to videos like this one get found. My last how-to on TikTok got over three hundred thousand views, and most of them came from people searching for it.

show.record: your TikTok analytics for the skeleton how-to: the 304K views, then the traffic source with 88% search

beats.say: So people clearly want to watch these. The hard part has always been making them.
So how do people make these? The honest answer: it's a lot of work.
You write a script, record a voice, draw or find more than a hundred pictures, and then line every one of them up with the voice in an editor.
Editors like After Effects and CapCut are great at that. But for a ten minute video, that's days of work, and that's exactly where most people give up.
I wanted a way where I only bring the idea. So I tried Zyvo's Long Form tool, and here's the whole process.
If you want to follow along, the link is in the description. You can try a preview first: it makes a title, an opening line and three sample scenes before you pay anything.
And if this ends up helping you, a like really does help this video reach more people.
Step one: type your idea.
Open Zyvo and click Long Form on the left.

show.record: from the Zyvo home page, click Long Form in the sidebar

beats.say: Now type what your video should be about. It doesn't need to be a perfect title. I'm going with: what if humans could breathe underwater?

show.record: Start with a topic: type "What if humans could breathe underwater?" slowly in the Video topic box

beats.say: If you don't have an idea yet, Discover ideas suggests some for you.

show.record: hover over Discover ideas (don't click it)

beats.say: It makes videos from eight to fifteen minutes. I'll leave the length on Auto and click Create Story Plan.

show.record: show Target length on Auto, then click Create Story Plan

beats.say: Step two: check the story.
A few seconds later you get a story plan: a title, the opening, and the chapters, written for this exact question.

show.record: the Story step as it appears: scroll slowly through the title, the opening and the chapters

beats.say: Read the opening line. This is the part that decides if people keep watching, so if it's not strong, change it here.

show.record: click into the opening line and change a word or two

beats.say: Scroll through the chapters too. If the story wanders, this is the cheapest place to fix it, before a single picture is drawn.

show.record: scroll back up through the chapters once more, slowly

beats.say: When you're happy with it, go on to the look.

show.record: click the button to the Look step

beats.say: Step three: pick a look.
There are six visual styles. The bold cartoon one is the closest to the videos we just saw, so that's the one I'll use.

show.record: the Look step: hover over each of the 6 styles, then pick the bold cartoon one

beats.say: Step four: generate.
Before it starts, it shows you exactly how many credits this video will cost. A full video needs a paid plan, so check this number first.

show.record: the Generate step with the credit cost visible, then click Generate

beats.say: Now it writes the full script, records the voice and draws every scene, and you can watch it work through them.

show.record: the progress screen while scenes appear (record a minute; the assembly uses the liveliest part)

beats.say: You don't have to sit and watch. You can close the tab and come back when it's done.
I won't lie: this part takes a while. Mine took [MINUTES] minutes from the click to the finished video, so this is a good moment to grab a coffee.

show.record: keep a clock or timer visible on screen from the Generate click to the end (or note the start and end time)

beats.say: Step five: fix any scene you don't like.
When it's done, every scene is in the editor. Mine has [SCENES] scenes; a ten minute video usually has about a hundred and fifty.

show.record: the editor of the finished video: scroll the scene strip slowly so the scene count shows

beats.say: Watch it through once. If a picture doesn't match what the voice says, open that scene and make it again, before you publish.

show.record: open one scene and redo its picture

beats.say: Then download the video.
So here's what I got. No editing from me at all.

show.record: the finished video (the same file as at the start)

beats.say: And the second one is faster, because now you know the five steps.
Type an idea, check the story, pick the look, generate, and fix any scene you don't like.
That's the real change for me: my time goes into finding good ideas, not into editing timelines.
Now, a few honest limits before you try it.
It's English only right now. And it doesn't upload to YouTube for you: you download the file and upload it yourself.
And always watch it before you publish. The pictures are made by AI, so check that every scene matches what's being said.
If you could make one of these about anything, what would your first "What if" be? Tell me in the comments, and I might make the best one next.
The link to Zyvo is in the description. Subscribe if you want to see what I try next.
